body.text: On November 19, the United Nations’ highest court delivered a landmark judgment, finding that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Nine years after fleeing genocide in Myanmar, over a million Rohingya refugees continue to live in the overcrowded refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. For the Rohingya, the ruling issued by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) was a historic day. It marked a moment of new hope in their long-waited struggle for recognition, accountability, and justice. It also brought a new surge of hope about finally returning home – something every Rohingya dreams of.

“When I was watching the first public hearing in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar from a tarpaulin shelter in 2019, I was very hopeful for justice. But since it took time and the situation got worse day by day, I thought justice had died,” Ro Anis Ahmed, executive director of Center for Social Development (CSD), told The Diplomat.
“Today, I feel that justice is still alive. The ICJ’s judgment in favor of The Gambia is a historic legal victory for us, but the real victory depends on its implementation.”

The ICJ accepted the estimate that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2017 military operations, and found at least 1,834 acts of rape. About 750 people were killed in Min Gyi (Tula Toli), 358 in Chut Pyin (including 127 children aged five or under), and at least 82 in Maung Nu. The court said the Chut Pyin figures could not be confirmed but are believable. It also examined seven other sites of serious violence, and found that Myanmar destroyed Rohingya villages in a planned way and later built security bases and other infrastructure on the land.

According to a report by MSF, over 700,000 Rohingya were driven out of Myanmar within a few weeks in 2017. The military’s atrocities – including murder, rape, and arson – forced Rohingya civilians to flee their homeland and seek refuge in Bangladesh.

The ICJ case, which began in 2019, has drawn international attention because the Myanmar military has now been officially found guilty of genocide against the Rohingya – the first time a state has been censured under the U.N. Genocide Convention.

Human rights organizations and U.N. reports documented widespread mass killings, brutal sexual violence and gang rapes, torture, and the systematic burning of entire Rohingya villages in 2017. There was no single, specific reason behind the military’s targeting of the Rohingya; rather, it was rooted in racism, discrimination, ethnic differences, and religious distinctions.

After the military launched its brutal crackdown, many Rohingya fled on foot through forests and hills, while others crossed the Naf River in small boats. Some spent more than a week walking to reach Bangladesh. Most of them entered through the Naf River in Teknaf. During that time, many lost family members, homes, and all their belongings; others perished attempting to cross the Naf River after their boats capsized.
Some Rohingya attempted to reach Malaysia and other neighboring countries by fishing boat, but many of these individuals have since gone missing.

Those who fled to Bangladesh in 2017 are living in dire conditions today, while those who managed to reach Malaysia are hiding to survive due to brutal treatment from the government. Meanwhile, the Rohingya remaining in Myanmar’s Rakhine State continue to face similar forms of persecution at the hands of the Arakan Army.

“The [ICJ’s] long overdue verdict is in our favor, but our plight is not over,” said Sirajul Islam, a Rohingya poet and writer. “Our plight and quest for justice ends when our hope for home translates into reality.”

On November 20, the day following the ICJ’s ruling on the genocide case, Dr. Khalilur Rahman, Bangladesh’s foreign minister as well as the president of the 81st session of the U.N. General Assembly, arrived with his delegation and other high-ranking officials from U.N. agencies and government in the Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar. They came to meet with Rohingya refugees and listen to their voices following the historic judgment.

A large gathering took place at Camp 4 football field, where Rohingya refugees had the opportunity to speak with the president of the U.N. General Assembly. During this visit, Rahman engaged with members of the Rohingya community to hear directly about their concerns and expectations.

The Rohingya community was overjoyed to see him back at the camp, as evidenced by banners adorned with his face. During his visit, Rahman stated that the Rohingya crisis is now a matter for the international community, and that the international community would work to address it as soon as possible. He expressed hope that the Rohingya would soon be able to return to their homes.
Rahman assured the refugees that he would return to the camp before long, bringing some good news.

This visit comes at a highly significant moment for the Rohingya community. While Myanmar remains a deeply hostile environment for Rohingya, international funding has caused drastic cuts to food and health care for the refugees.

Now the ICJ ruling opens a crucial opportunity in their pursuit of justice and a means to ensure their voices are heard. This ruling can’t give back the loved ones they lost, nor can it erase their memories. But it offers the community a new hope that justice is indeed possible. It is a historic moment for the Rohingya.

Enous Juhar, a Rohingya survivor of the 2017 violence, was forced to flee his home in Myanmar after the military’s brutal operations. He described his emotions after hearing the ruling: “Although I have lost my home and everything I had in my homeland, I remain hopeful today that justice is nearer, those responsible will be held accountable, and our suffering will be acknowledged, while also creating the path for our return to our own land by ensuring our safety, rights, and citizenship.”

Human rights activists have welcomed this ruling and are calling for concrete steps to be taken to ensure accountability, bring perpetrators to justice, and safeguard the rights and future of the Rohingya population.

For the Rohingya, justice would mean acknowledging their suffering, establishing accountability, and ensuring that such crimes never happen again and no criminal goes unpunished. But more than that, they also dream of a future where every Rohingya can live without fear and return to their homeland.

“The Myanmar military killed my father in 2017. Even now without my father, we continue to suffer in the camp,” said Amir Hossain, a 50-year-old Rohingya refugee. “Now all we want is to return home with full rights, safety, and citizenship.”

While survivors continue to carry the trauma of that violence, young Rohingya are growing up in refugee camps having never had the chance to set their feet on the soil of their homeland. Many young people have spent a significant portion of their lives in camps, where they face severe restrictions on freedom of movement and other basic rights. With a lack of higher education, there are limited opportunities for Rohingya youth.

In April 2026, the World Food Program (WFP) was forced to further reduce already limited rations. Consequently, some Rohingya refugees, particularly the youth, are engaging in criminal activities to survive. The elderly and children suffer from malnutrition and families struggle to sustain themselves.
For Rohingya refugees, pursuing justice is deeply linked not only to the suffering of the past but also to their future.

The Rohingya community’s message is clear: They have waited too long. Nine years is more than enough. They are not asking for sympathy; they are asking for justice. They don’t want to see another generation growing in the camp. All they want is to return home, but the return must be safe with full rights, citizenship, and dignity.
A Rohingya youth activist, Anowar Faisel, said that justice means being recognized as a human being with the same rights, dignity, and freedom as people in other communities.

Bangladesh has attempted to repatriate the Rohingya twice and continues to seek help from the international community and world leaders – so far, with nothing to show for the effort. According to recent reports, Bangladesh is engaging in discussions with both the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army – the insurgent group that currently controls Rakhine State – to explore ways to repatriate the Rohingya.

However, the Rohingya community and rights activists stress that repatriation is not possible at present given the escalated civil war currently spreading out in Rakhine State. The ongoing conflict between the Myanmar military and the AA is resulting in the continuous loss of life among Rohingya civilians, with both parties targeting them. The military and the AA have been accused of forcibly recruiting the Rohingya to join their war efforts, while committing the same types of abuses seen on a larger scale in 2017.

Rohingya leaders say that the international community must come together and act to ensure accountability for those responsible, support justice for survivors, and put pressure on Myanmar to guarantee the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of Rohingya refugees with citizenship and full rights.

As the court read out its judgment, Rohingya refugees sheltered in Bangladesh watched intently. Now they wait to see the next steps, hoping to return to their homes, reunite with their loved ones, and rebuild their lives. The international community should demonstrate that justice is for all, that no one is above the law, and that humanity is still alive. And that means the world must find a solution to the Rohingya issue.
